questions.title: Is the entropy definition in Eq. (1) missing a minus sign?
questions.question_body:
In Section 2.3 (Entropy Patching), entropy is defined as

$H(x_i) = \sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}} p_e(x_i=v\mid \mathbf{x}_{<i}) \log p_e(x_i=v\mid \mathbf{x}_{<i})$.

Standard Shannon entropy is $-\sum p \log p$. Without the negative sign, $H(x_i)$ would be non-positive and larger uncertainty would correspond to more negative values. Yet, the thresholding rules later compare $H(x_t)$ to positive thresholds $\theta_g$ and $\theta_r$. Is the minus sign omitted unintentionally, or are you using a different convention (e.g., negative entropy)? If it is a different convention, how should I interpret the threshold values and the statements about “high entropy” boundaries?

questions.title: How exactly is the patch boundary decided at inference time without future context?
questions.question_body: The paper states that the patching function must be incremental, i.e., $f_p(\mathbf{x}_{<i}) = f_p(\mathbf{x})_{<i}$. During generation, the model needs to decide whether position $i$ starts a new patch before any future bytes are known. When using entropy-based patching, do you run the same small entropy LM causally on the already generated prefix and then apply the same global or approximate monotonicity rule with a fixed threshold? If the inference threshold is sometimes tuned (e.g., from 0.6 to 0.1 in Section 4.2), is this tuning performed globally per task, per sequence, or adaptively during decoding? How do you avoid introducing a mismatch between training and inference patch boundaries?

questions.title: Clarifying the "approximate monotonicity constraint": why use a positive jump condition?
questions.question_body: In Section 2.3 you define a boundary when $H(x_t) - H(x_{t-1}) > \theta_r$, motivated as breaking a roughly monotonically decreasing entropy within a patch. My intuition is that entropy is high at the start of a word and tends to decrease, so a large positive jump $H_t - H_{t-1}$ would indicate entropy is increasing again, suggesting a new hard region. But then wouldn't the first high-entropy byte of a patch also need a rule to start that patch? Do you combine the relative jump rule with a global threshold $H_t > \theta_g$, or can the relative rule alone seed a new patch at the beginning of a word-like unit? Could you provide a concrete example trace of $H_i$ where both rules trigger boundaries and explain why?

questions.title: How does BLT decide when to invoke the global transformer during generation?
questions.question_body: The text says the global latent transformer runs on patch representations and dominates FLOPs, and that deciding whether a position is a patch boundary controls whether we invoke it. In autoregressive decoding, is the control flow literally: generate next byte(s) with the local decoder conditioned on the last latent state until a boundary is signaled, then run the global transformer one step to produce the next latent output, and resume local decoding? If so, how do you prevent drift if the local decoder makes an unexpected byte that changes the entropy landscape compared to training-time boundaries?

questions.title: Reconciling batch packing: are you fixing bytes per batch or patches per batch?
questions.question_body: Section 3.3 says you keep the number of bytes per batch constant in expectation to equalize context across patch sizes. Later it says: "for efficiency, our implementation packs batches of patches to avoid padding ... This ensures that every batch has the same number of patches." These seem at odds: constant bytes-per-batch vs constant patches-per-batch. Which quantity is actually fixed during training steps that are compared, and how do you ensure fairness when dynamic patching changes the byte-to-patch ratio across sequences?

questions.title: What does the cross-attention pooling function f do, and where is max-pooling used?
questions.question_body: In the Local Encoder section, the cross-attention query initialization uses a pooling function $f$ over the bytes of a patch, followed by a projection. Later, Section 3.10 mentions you use max-pooling to initialize the queries for the first encoder cross-attention layer. Is max-pooling used only at the first layer and some other pooling at later layers, or is max-pooling consistent across all encoder layers? If the latter, what happens to gradient flow and stability compared to mean pooling, and did you observe differences for larger patch sizes?

questions.title: Dimensional consistency in encoder cross-attention: why maintain multi-head states at $h_\mathcal{E}$?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.2.2 you mention that patch representations are typically of dimension $h_\mathcal{G}$, while byte representations are $h_\mathcal{E}$. During encoder cross-attention you keep the per-head dimensionality at $h_\mathcal{E}$, maintain multiple heads, and only later concatenate to $h_\mathcal{G}$. Could you illustrate the exact tensor shapes for $Q$, $K$, $V$, and $P_l$ through one cross-attention block and clarify the role of $k$ (the number of splits) in mapping from $h_\mathcal{E}$ heads to the final $h_\mathcal{G}$ patch vector?

questions.title: What is the precise training objective and factorization across local and global modules?
questions.question_body: Is the loss strictly the byte-level autoregressive cross-entropy on the local decoder outputs with vocabulary size 256 (as suggested by $V=256$ in the FLOPs formula)? If so, is there any auxiliary loss on the encoder or the latent global outputs (e.g., reconstruction, contrastive, or KL)? How is teacher forcing implemented across patch boundaries during training to ensure the global latent transformer learns long-range structure while the local decoder handles byte-level detail?

questions.title: How are patch boundaries supervised during training if patching is dynamic?
questions.question_body: For entropy patching, boundaries are computed by a small byte LM. Are those boundaries treated as fixed labels during BLT training, or are they updated on-the-fly if the BLT’s own predictions would alter entropies? If the entropy model is trained on the same data, does using it to define boundaries risk overfitting or leakage of data-specific segmentation biases into BLT? Did you experiment with training the entropy model on a disjoint subset or freezing it early to prevent drift?

questions.title: Understanding "entropy drift" and the context reset heuristic
questions.question_body: Section 3.5 mentions "entropy drift" where repeated content in long contexts causes progressively larger patches. You mitigate this by resetting the entropy model's context at newlines and preferring the approximate monotonicity rule. Could you quantify how much this changes the patch length distribution on structured tasks (e.g., MMLU), and whether it harms performance on free-form text? More broadly, does this indicate the entropy model is overly sensitive to far-past context, and would a shorter receptive field be a better general solution?

questions.title: Can you clarify the FLOPs-per-byte equation and the roles of m, r, k, and n_p?
questions.question_body:
In Section 3.6 the FLOPs per byte for BLT sums several Transformer and Cross-Attention terms. I am confused by the symbols:

- $n_{ctx}$ is bytes per sequence, $n_p$ is patch size (average bytes per patch), but Transf.FL for the global model uses $m=n_{ctx}/n_p$ as the sequence length in patches.
- $k$ is "the number of local model splits that concatenate to form a global model representation" and is set to 2 in the figure.
- For cross-attention, you have terms like CrossAttn.FL$(h_\mathcal{E}, l_\mathcal{E}, m=n_p, r=n_p/k)\times k/n_p$ and CrossAttn.FL$(h_\mathcal{D}, l_\mathcal{D}, m=k, r=k/n_p)$.

Could you provide a small worked example with concrete numbers (e.g., $n_{ctx}=8192$, average patch size $n_p=4$, $k=2$) to show how many queries and key/values each cross-attention sees per layer and how those $m$ and $r$ map to actual attention matrix sizes?

questions.title: Equalizing context length across patch sizes: is there still an advantage from longer effective context?
questions.question_body: You state that to avoid giving larger patch sizes an unfair advantage, you keep the number of bytes per sequence fixed in expectation and reduce the number of transformer steps when patches are longer. However, the global transformer’s receptive field over patches might still cover different semantic extents depending on segmentation. For example, a model with longer patches could see more words per global step if easy regions are merged. How do you rule out that such implicit context changes are not driving the observed improvements, especially in the fixed-inference scaling experiments?

questions.title: What prevents the local decoder from overfitting to frequent byte n-grams and ignoring the latent?
questions.question_body: Since the local decoder predicts bytes conditioned on both past bytes and the current patch’s latent representation, how do you ensure the latent signal is used rather than the decoder memorizing local byte patterns? Do you ablate the decoder capacity or vary the encoder/decoder layer counts to show that performance drops if the latent is weakened? Any diagnostics like attention weights from bytes to latents demonstrating information flow?

questions.title: Hash n-gram embeddings: how severe are collisions and how are sizes chosen?
questions.question_body: The encoder uses hash embeddings for $n$-grams with a single hash function and tables of around 500k entries across $n\in\{3,\dots,8\}$. What is the expected collision rate for typical $n$-gram distributions in your corpora, and did you test multiple independent hashes or larger tables to reduce collisions? How sensitive are downstream results to collisions, and is there a principled way to choose table sizes given a target collision probability and memory budget?

questions.title: Why does BLT sometimes start worse than BPE at small scales but surpass it at larger scales?
questions.question_body: In Section 4.1 you note that BLT with average patch size 8 underperforms BPE at 1B but surpasses BPE by 7B. Is this primarily due to the local encoder/decoder constituting a larger fraction of total parameters at small scales, thus limiting representational power, while at larger scales the global transformer dominates? Could you quantify the parameter and FLOP shares of local vs global modules at each scale to substantiate this explanation?

questions.title: Classification likelihood scoring with bytes vs tokens: how is BPB made comparable?
questions.question_body: For classification tasks, you compute likelihood over choice characters and report accuracy. Since BLT operates over bytes, the likelihood of a choice string depends on byte segmentation and local decoding steps, while BPE models score over tokens. How do you ensure fair comparison, e.g., are prompts and choices exactly the same strings and does scoring normalize over different lengths? Also, when reporting BPB for language modeling, are text normalizations and newline conventions identical across models, to avoid artifacts from differing byte boundaries?

questions.title: How is the block-causal attention mask defined for the global transformer when patches vary in size?
questions.question_body: You mention using a block-causal mask that restricts attention up to and including the current patch, within the current document. When patches have variable length, is the mask simply causal over the patch index (i.e., a 1D sequence of patch tokens), ignoring the within-patch byte positions? If so, does the global model ever see any fine-grained positional signal about where within a patch a salient pattern occurs, or is that entirely delegated to the local modules?

questions.title: Is BPE really non-incremental in practice, and could a simple delimiter make it comparable?
questions.question_body: You argue BPE is non-incremental because tokenization of a prefix can change with future context, violating $f_p(\mathbf{x}_{<i}) = f_p(\mathbf{x})_{<i}$. But you note that adding a special delimiter token could make BPE incremental at the cost of longer sequences. Did you quantify how much longer sequences would get if such delimiters are inserted at intended patch boundaries, and how that would compare to BLT’s FLOP and performance trade-offs? Would delimiter-augmented BPE reduce the robustness gap you see on character-level tasks?

questions.title: Entropy model training and generalization: does training on the same data introduce bias?
questions.question_body: The entropy model is trained on the same data distribution as BLT and then used to segment training and evaluation inputs. Could this coupling bias segmentation toward patterns the entropy model has memorized, thereby overfitting the patching to the training distribution? Did you try training the entropy model on a different corpus or earlier fraction of the data and freezing it? How sensitive are results to mismatches between entropy model domain and downstream task domain?

questions.title: Fixed-inference scaling: how do you fairly trade off patch size against model size?
questions.question_body: In Section 4.3 you scale both patch size and global model size while holding inference FLOPs constant, and BLT scales better than BPE. Could you detail the exact accounting: which FLOP components shrink with larger patches (global steps), which remain fixed (local encoder/decoder per-byte work), and how you choose the new global depth/width to match a target inference budget? A small table with FLOP terms before and after would clarify where the gains come from.

questions.title: Does the local decoder’s output vocabulary of 256 bytes limit multilingual performance?
questions.question_body: BLT decodes raw bytes with $V=256$. For scripts with multi-byte UTF-8 code points, the model must learn byte-level patterns corresponding to characters and sub-characters. Did you observe any degradation on languages with complex scripts compared to BPE models that can allocate whole-character tokens? Your FLORES-101 results suggest gains in low-resource settings; could you share per-script error analyses that reveal whether BLT systematically benefits or struggles with certain byte patterns?
